Weights and robust standard errors

Source: vignettes/articles/weights.Rmd
weights.Rmd
library(anovakit)

Three functions take prior weights and four take a robust covariance.

Which functions take weights

Function weights vcov_type
anova_bin() yes yes
anova_count() yes yes
anova_glm() yes yes
anova_ancova() no yes

weights names a numeric column of the data, not a vector. The weights are then subsetted with the rows, so they stay aligned when a row is dropped for a missing value; a vector evaluated against the original data would not. The column must be numeric and non-negative, and it cannot also be the response, a grouping column or the offset. A missing or infinite weight is treated like a missing value in any other analysed column: the row is dropped and counted in $n_removed.

How the weights are read

What a weight means depends on the weights and on the response. The package decides which reading applies and says so in $notes when the reading changes a result: the Pearson dispersion in anova_count(), the robust covariance, and weights that are not whole numbers.

The weights are On Read as Each row is
whole numbers, some above 1 a 0/1 response (binomial, quasi-binomial) or counts (Poisson, quasi-Poisson, negative binomial) frequency weights that many identical observations
whole numbers a proportion (binomial) numbers of trials one binomial observation
not all whole numbers, or any weights in another family any response weights used as given, as glm() uses them one unit

anova_bin() always has a 0/1 response and anova_count() always has counts, so in those two functions whole-number weights are always frequencies. anova_glm() also takes proportions, where whole-number weights are trials, and the Gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian and quasi() families, where they are precision weights. In both cases each row stays one unit.

Frequency weights

A frequency weight says how many identical observations a row stands for. UCBAdmissions is a table of 4,526 applications to graduate school at Berkeley in 1973, by gender, department and outcome. As a data frame it has one row per cell and the count in Freq:

ucb <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucb)
#>      Admit Gender Dept Freq
#> 1 Admitted   Male    A  512
#> 2 Rejected   Male    A  313
#> 3 Admitted Female    A   89
#> 4 Rejected Female    A   19
#> 5 Admitted   Male    B  353
#> 6 Rejected   Male    B  207
c(rows = nrow(ucb), applicants = sum(ucb$Freq))
#>       rows applicants 
#>         24       4526

For comparison, here is the same data with one row per applicant:

applicants <- ucb[rep(seq_len(nrow(ucb)), ucb$Freq),
                  c("Admit", "Gender", "Dept")]
row.names(applicants) <- NULL
nrow(applicants)
#> [1] 4526

The 24-row table with weights = "Freq" and the 4,526 rows without weights give the same analysis:

from_table <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                        success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
from_rows <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                       success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
all.equal(from_table$anova, from_rows$anova)
#> [1] TRUE
data.frame(comparison = from_table$effect_sizes$comparison,
           or_table = from_table$effect_sizes$odds_ratio,
           or_rows = from_rows$effect_sizes$odds_ratio,
           se_table = from_table$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           se_rows = from_rows$effect_sizes$se_log_or)
#>       comparison   or_table    or_rows   se_table    se_rows
#> 1 Female vs Male 1.10502735 1.10502735 0.08084646 0.08084644
#> 2         B vs A 0.95753028 0.95753028 0.10983890 0.10983890
#> 3         C vs A 0.28291804 0.28291804 0.10663289 0.10663288
#> 4         D vs A 0.27400567 0.27400567 0.10582342 0.10582342
#> 5         E vs A 0.17564230 0.17564230 0.12611350 0.12611349
#> 6         F vs A 0.03664494 0.03664494 0.16998176 0.16998115
c(table = from_table$model_stats$BIC, rows = from_rows$model_stats$BIC)
#>    table     rows 
#> 5246.412 5246.412

The odds ratios and standard errors agree to about six significant figures; the rest is glm()’s convergence tolerance. BIC agrees too, because with frequency weights its penalty uses the 4,526 observations the weights represent, not the 24 rows. The marginal means, the comparisons and the observed proportions in $assumptions$proportions match in the same way.

Counts work the same way in anova_count(). InsectSprays has 72 insect counts, 12 for each of six sprays. Tabulated, it becomes one row per spray and count, with the frequency in Freq:

spray_tab <- as.data.frame(table(spray = InsectSprays$spray,
                                 count = InsectSprays$count),
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
spray_tab$count <- as.numeric(spray_tab$count)
c(rows = nrow(spray_tab), nonzero_rows = sum(spray_tab$Freq > 0),
  observations = sum(spray_tab$Freq))
#>         rows nonzero_rows observations 
#>          144           43           72
spray_rows <- anova_count(InsectSprays, "count", "spray", plots = FALSE)
spray_freq <- anova_count(spray_tab, "count", "spray", weights = "Freq",
                          plots = FALSE)
c(rows = spray_rows$model_type, table = spray_freq$model_type)
#>     rows    table 
#> "negbin" "negbin"
c(rows = spray_rows$dispersion, table = spray_freq$dispersion)
#>     rows    table 
#> 1.507713 1.507713
all.equal(spray_rows$anova, spray_freq$anova)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(spray_rows$effect_sizes, spray_freq$effect_sizes)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(spray_rows$emmeans, spray_freq$emmeans)
#> [1] TRUE
grep("frequency weights", spray_freq$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "The weights in `Freq` are whole numbers, so they are treated as frequency weights: each row stands for that many observations. The Pearson dispersion divides by the 72 observations they represent minus the 6 parameters, not by the 43 rows, which would inflate it."

The Pearson dispersion, on which model = "auto" chooses between Poisson and negative binomial, divides by the observations minus the parameters. Divided by the rows of the table instead, it would be larger, and could switch the model for no reason in the data. In anova_glm() the residual degrees of freedom are counted in observations in the same way, so a quasi-Poisson or quasi-binomial fit, an F test and a t interval on a frequency table equal those of the expanded data. $model is still the glm that stats::glm() fitted to the rows, and $notes says when its own summary() would differ.

The counts walkthrough shows the $assumptions$cell_counts table and the observed plot for a frequency table.

Zero weights

spray_tab above still holds the combinations of spray and count that never occurred, with a frequency of zero. A row with weight zero contributes nothing to the fit, so it is dropped before fitting and counted in $n_removed:

c(supplied = nrow(spray_tab), used = nrow(spray_freq$data_used),
  removed = spray_freq$n_removed)
#> supplied     used  removed 
#>      144       43      101
grep("zero", spray_freq$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Dropped 101 row(s) whose weight in `Freq` is zero: they contribute nothing to the fit, and keeping them would make row counts, robust standard errors and information criteria disagree with it."

Keeping those rows would make the row counts, the robust standard errors and the information criteria disagree with the fit. As for every function, nrow($data_used) + $n_removed is the number of rows supplied.

A group whose weights are all zero is dropped from the analysis, and the note names it:

no_f <- spray_tab
no_f$Freq[no_f$spray == "F"] <- 0
grep("Level", anova_count(no_f, "count", "spray", weights = "Freq",
                          plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Level \"F\" of `spray` had no rows with a non-zero weight in `Freq`, so it was dropped from the analysis."

When every weight is zero, or only one row has a non-zero weight, the function stops with an error.

Trials behind proportions

A binomial response can be given as a proportion, with the number of trials behind each proportion as the weight. That form is for anova_glm(): anova_bin() takes a 0/1 response only. esoph is a case-control study of oesophageal cancer, with the numbers of cases and controls in each of 88 combinations of age group, alcohol and tobacco consumption:

es <- esoph
es$agegp <- factor(es$agegp, ordered = FALSE)
es$alcgp <- factor(es$alcgp, ordered = FALSE)
es$trials <- es$ncases + es$ncontrols
es$prop <- es$ncases / es$trials
head(es[, c("agegp", "alcgp", "ncases", "trials", "prop")])
#>   agegp     alcgp ncases trials prop
#> 1 25-34 0-39g/day      0     40    0
#> 2 25-34 0-39g/day      0     10    0
#> 3 25-34 0-39g/day      0      6    0
#> 4 25-34 0-39g/day      0      5    0
#> 5 25-34     40-79      0     27    0
#> 6 25-34     40-79      0      7    0

(The factors are made unordered so that the coefficients are comparisons with the first level rather than polynomial trends.) With one row per subject instead, the same data have 975 rows of a 0/1 response:

per_subject <- rbind(
  data.frame(agegp = rep(es$agegp, es$ncases),
             alcgp = rep(es$alcgp, es$ncases), case = 1),
  data.frame(agegp = rep(es$agegp, es$ncontrols),
             alcgp = rep(es$alcgp, es$ncontrols), case = 0))
nrow(per_subject)
#> [1] 975
as_prop <- anova_glm(es, "prop", c("agegp", "alcgp"), family = binomial(),
                     weights = "trials", plots = FALSE)
as_rows <- anova_glm(per_subject, "case", c("agegp", "alcgp"),
                     family = binomial(), plots = FALSE)
all.equal(as_prop$anova, as_rows$anova)
#> [1] TRUE
data.frame(term = as_prop$emmeans$term,
           level = ifelse(is.na(as_prop$emmeans$agegp),
                          as.character(as_prop$emmeans$alcgp),
                          as.character(as_prop$emmeans$agegp)),
           prob_prop = as_prop$emmeans$estimate,
           prob_rows = as_rows$emmeans$estimate)
#>     term     level  prob_prop  prob_rows
#> 1  agegp     25-34 0.01253232 0.01253232
#> 2  agegp     35-44 0.06089869 0.06089869
#> 3  agegp     45-54 0.28070062 0.28070062
#> 4  agegp     55-64 0.39570900 0.39570900
#> 5  agegp     65-74 0.49748585 0.49748585
#> 6  agegp       75+ 0.51434499 0.51434499
#> 7  alcgp 0-39g/day 0.03978680 0.03978680
#> 8  alcgp     40-79 0.14813421 0.14813421
#> 9  alcgp    80-119 0.23568034 0.23568034
#> 10 alcgp      120+ 0.62161114 0.62161114

The likelihood-ratio tests and the marginal means are the same. The deviance explained is not: it is measured against the saturated model, which differs between the two forms, and a note says so. McFadden’s R squared is computed from the Bernoulli log-likelihood and is the same either way.

The trials are not frequencies, because each row is one binomial observation rather than a count of identical ones. The Pearson dispersion of the proportions carries information about overdispersion, which a 0/1 response cannot show, so anova_glm() checks it:

as_prop$assumptions$dispersion
#> [1] 1.487358
grep("Pearson dispersion", as_prop$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Pearson dispersion is 1.49 (Pearson test of overdispersion: p = 0.0032), where a binomial model assumes 1: its test statistics are inflated by about that factor, its standard errors are about 1.22 times too small, and a nominal 5% test on 1 degree of freedom rejects roughly 11% of true null hypotheses, and one on 5 (the largest term here) roughly 19%. Consider family = \"quasibinomial\", or a beta-binomial model."

A robust covariance also treats each of the 88 rows as one unit, so it allows for the extra variation between rows that the dispersion of 1.49 measures. The per-subject form cannot see that variation, and its robust standard errors stay close to the model-based ones:

prop_hc3 <- anova_glm(es, "prop", c("agegp", "alcgp"), family = binomial(),
                      weights = "trials", vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
rows_hc3 <- anova_glm(per_subject, "case", c("agegp", "alcgp"),
                      family = binomial(), vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
data.frame(term = as_prop$emmeans$term,
           se_model = as_prop$emmeans$se,
           se_hc3_prop = prop_hc3$emmeans$se,
           se_hc3_rows = rows_hc3$emmeans$se)
#>     term   se_model se_hc3_prop se_hc3_rows
#> 1  agegp 0.01262372  0.01385063 0.012971823
#> 2  agegp 0.02058721  0.02866157 0.020267469
#> 3  agegp 0.03880783  0.04939598 0.036329909
#> 4  agegp 0.03980602  0.06202781 0.043375963
#> 5  agegp 0.04952135  0.06751124 0.052921400
#> 6  agegp 0.09561464  0.12208635 0.093769792
#> 7  alcgp 0.01013718  0.01385172 0.009974735
#> 8  alcgp 0.02836986  0.03417081 0.028016447
#> 9  alcgp 0.04783171  0.05382355 0.046929813
#> 10 alcgp 0.08038267  0.11456357 0.093728591

Trials do not inflate the tests the way unequal sampling weights do (below): they set the variance of each proportion, as precision weights do.

Sampling and other weights that are not whole numbers

Weights that are not whole numbers are used as given, as stats::glm() uses prior weights: each row’s contribution to the likelihood is multiplied by its weight, as if it were that many observations. The fit, the tests, the intervals and the marginal means all treat them that way. The robust covariance treats each row as one unit instead, and two checks rescale the weights to average 1 first: the sparse-data check of anova_bin() and the Pearson dispersion on which anova_count() chooses its model.

Suppose the applicants above came from a survey that sampled men at a higher rate than women, so that each woman’s response is weighted up and each man’s down. The weights here are made up for illustration and average 1:

applicants$w <- c(Male = 0.4, Female = 2.2)[as.character(applicants$Gender)]
applicants$w <- applicants$w / mean(applicants$w)
tapply(applicants$w, applicants$Gender, unique)
#>      Male    Female 
#> 0.3540501 1.9472758

Their scale matters

Weights used as given have no natural scale, and the tests scale with them. The same weights divided by 100 make the 4,526 applicants count as about 45, and every likelihood-ratio statistic falls by the same factor:

sw <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "w",
                success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
applicants$w_small <- applicants$w / 100
sw_small <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                      weights = "w_small", success = "Admitted",
                      plots = FALSE)
data.frame(term = sw$anova$term, mean_1 = sw$anova$statistic,
           mean_0.01 = sw_small$anova$statistic)
#>     term     mean_1  mean_0.01
#> 1 Gender   6.100007 0.06100007
#> 2   Dept 684.795658 6.84795658
grep("average", sw_small$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "The weights in `w_small` are not all whole numbers, so they are not read as frequencies, and they average 0.01 rather than 1. The fit, the tests and the intervals use them as given, as glm() uses prior weights, so their scale matters: multiplying every weight by a constant multiplies each likelihood-ratio and Wald statistic by about that constant. For sampling weights, rescale them to average 1, or use a design-based method such as survey::svyglm()."
#> [2] "The grouping factors enter the model additively, so $emmeans and $posthoc are reported for each factor separately, averaged over the others (column `term`), and each factor's comparisons are a separate multiplicity family. Set interaction = TRUE to compare cells instead."

anova_bin(), anova_count() and a Poisson or binomial anova_glm() give that note whenever such weights do not average 1 (within about 10%). Rescale sampling weights to average 1, as above, or analyse them with a design-based method such as survey::svyglm().

In a binomial model, weights that are not whole numbers also make AIC, BIC and the log-likelihood in $model_stats NA, with a note, because R’s binomial log-likelihood rounds the weights. McFadden’s R squared and the model-versus-null test use the deviances and are reported. glm()’s warning about “non-integer #successes” is recorded in $notes rather than printed.

In anova_count() the Pearson dispersion in $dispersion and $model_dispersion is computed with the weights rescaled to average 1, so the choice between Poisson and negative binomial does not depend on their scale. In anova_glm() the dispersion is that of the model as weighted, so in a Poisson or binomial fit it scales with the weights, and so does the overdispersion check; the note on the weights’ scale says so. A family that estimates its dispersion (Gaussian, Gamma, quasi families) absorbs the scale of the weights.

Unequal weights distort the tests

Weights that average 1 still distort the tests when they are unequal: some terms are inflated, others deflated. A likelihood-ratio or Wald test treats a woman’s row, of weight 1.95, as that many independent observations, while it is one person. How much that moves a test depends on where the heavy rows fall, so $notes computes the factor for each term from the sandwich covariance:

sw$anova
#>     term df  statistic       p_value
#> 1 Gender  1   6.100007  1.351813e-02
#> 2   Dept  5 684.795658 9.518615e-146
grep("unequal", sw$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "The weights in `w` are unequal and not frequencies, so the likelihood-ratio tests in $anova are inflated by between about 0.84 and 1.45, depending on the term (the weights are used as given and are not frequencies; computed from the sandwich covariance, assuming the weights are not inverse variances, which would not inflate them): a nominal 5% test of Dept rejects roughly 18% of true null hypotheses. The standard errors in the other tables are too small for the same reason; vcov_type = \"HC3\" gives ones that are not."

The calculation assumes the weights are not inverse variances; precision weights, such as the trials behind a proportion, would not inflate the tests. The note appears in anova_bin(), anova_count() and anova_glm() for Poisson, quasi-Poisson, negative binomial, binomial and quasi-binomial fits (on a binomial, only for weights that are not whole numbers on a 0/1 response). It never appears for Gaussian, Gamma or inverse Gaussian fits, where weights are read as precision weights. It is given only when some test would reject 7.5% or more of true null hypotheses at a nominal 5%. Under the quasi families’ F tests the estimated dispersion removes the average inflation but not the part due to unequal weights, and the note says so.

The remedy the note names is a robust covariance, and an omnibus test that uses it:

sw_hc3 <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "w",
                    success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3",
                    test_statistic = "Wald", plots = FALSE)
sw_hc3$anova
#>     term df  statistic      p_value
#> 1 Gender  1   7.388409 6.564554e-03
#> 2   Dept  5 396.687392 1.535320e-83
data.frame(comparison = sw$effect_sizes$comparison,
           se_model = sw$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           se_hc3 = sw_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or)
#>       comparison  se_model     se_hc3
#> 1 Female vs Male 0.1011743 0.09088179
#> 2         B vs A 0.1663584 0.14146922
#> 3         C vs A 0.1261355 0.13566444
#> 4         D vs A 0.1293345 0.13779505
#> 5         E vs A 0.1381565 0.15597408
#> 6         F vs A 0.1775987 0.21164049
grep("unequal", sw_hc3$notes, value = TRUE)
#> character(0)

Dept, the term the note names as the worst affected (its factor is the larger one), falls from 685 to 397; Gender rises from 6.10 to 7.39. Those are the directions of the note’s factors, but the sizes differ from them, because the comparison also moves from a likelihood-ratio to a Wald statistic. Most standard errors grow, and the inflation note is gone. Weights alone do not describe strata or clusters; a design-based analysis with survey accounts for those too.

Robust standard errors with vcov_type

vcov_type = "model" (the default) uses the model’s own covariance. "HC0" to "HC4" use a heteroscedasticity-consistent (sandwich) covariance from the sandwich package, which does not rely on the family’s variance function or on equal residual variances. HC0 is White’s estimator; HC1 to HC4 refine it for small samples, HC1 by a degrees-of-freedom factor and HC2 to HC4 by each row’s leverage. HC3, the default of sandwich::vcovHC() and the type used throughout this guide, is the usual choice for small or unbalanced groups.

The robust covariance does not reach every table:

Result anova_ancova() anova_bin() anova_count() anova_glm()
Coefficients no coefficient table $effect_sizes (odds ratios) $effect_sizes (rate ratios) $assumptions$coefficients
$emmeans and $posthoc yes yes yes yes
Omnibus $anova yes, as Wald F tests with test_statistic = "Wald" with test_statistic = "Wald" with test_statistic = "Wald"
$simple_slopes yes no such table no such table no such table
Not reached $effect_sizes, $slopes_test $anova unless test_statistic = "Wald" $anova unless test_statistic = "Wald"; $dispersion and the model choice $anova unless test_statistic = "Wald"; $effect_sizes

In anova_bin(), anova_count() and anova_glm(), a likelihood-ratio or F test compares deviances, so it rests on the model-based variance whatever vcov_type says; set test_statistic = "Wald" for an omnibus test that uses the robust covariance. $notes says which tests use it. Coefficient intervals in anova_bin() and anova_glm() become Wald intervals built from it, since a profile likelihood cannot use a sandwich covariance.

On warpbreaks (numbers of warp breaks per loom, 9 looms in each of six cells), the default likelihood-ratio table is unchanged by vcov_type, while a Wald table uses it:

breaks_model <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                            interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)
breaks_lr <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                         interaction = TRUE, vcov_type = "HC3",
                         plots = FALSE)
breaks_wald <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                           interaction = TRUE, vcov_type = "HC3",
                           test_statistic = "Wald", plots = FALSE)
all.equal(breaks_model$anova, breaks_lr$anova)
#> [1] TRUE
breaks_wald$anova
#>           term df statistic      p_value
#> 1         wool  1  2.526565 0.1119436981
#> 2      tension  2 16.808766 0.0002238839
#> 3 wool:tension  2  6.765016 0.0339621730
data.frame(comparison = breaks_model$effect_sizes$comparison,
           low_model = breaks_model$effect_sizes$conf_low,
           high_model = breaks_model$effect_sizes$conf_high,
           low_hc3 = breaks_lr$effect_sizes$conf_low,
           high_hc3 = breaks_lr$effect_sizes$conf_high)
#>              comparison low_model high_model   low_hc3  high_hc3
#> 1 B vs A at tension = L 0.4651349  0.8625808 0.4369807 0.9181560
#> 2    M vs L at wool = A 0.3938590  0.7366784 0.3696585 0.7849066
#> 3    H vs L at wool = A 0.4032354  0.7532465 0.3679333 0.8255184
#> 4   (B vs A) x (M vs L) 1.2122753  2.9560520 1.1459874 3.1270404
#> 5   (B vs A) x (H vs L) 0.7667100  1.9009866 0.7290004 1.9993205
grep("omnibus", breaks_lr$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "The omnibus likelihood-ratio test compares deviances, so it rests on the model-based variance; the robust (HC3) covariance is used only by $effect_sizes, the marginal means and the comparisons. For an omnibus test that uses it, set test_statistic = \"Wald\"."

In anova_ancova() the omnibus table itself changes: its F tests become Wald F tests built from the robust covariance (through car::Anova(vcov. = )), on the model’s residual degrees of freedom, so the table has no sums of squares. Its statistic attribute, which print() shows in the heading, says so. MASS::anorexia has the weights of 72 young women before and after one of three treatments:

an <- MASS::anorexia
an_hc3 <- anova_ancova(an, "Postwt", "Treat", "Prewt",
                       force_interaction = TRUE, vcov_type = "HC3",
                       plots = FALSE)
an_hc3$anova
#>          term df statistic     p_value
#> 1       Prewt  1  4.733147 0.033172900
#> 2       Treat  2  7.529746 0.001133501
#> 3 Prewt:Treat  2  3.211929 0.046650376
#> 4   Residuals 66        NA          NA
attr(an_hc3$anova, "statistic")
#> [1] "Wald F with HC3 covariance"
grep("Wald F", an_hc3$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "vcov_type = \"HC3\": the F tests in $anova are Wald F tests built from that covariance (car::Anova(vcov. = )), on the model's residual degrees of freedom, so the table has no sums of squares. $effect_sizes are still computed from the model-based sums of squares, which the covariance does not change, and the homogeneity-of-slopes test in $slopes_test is the model-based F test."

$effect_sizes are still computed from the model-based sums of squares, which the covariance does not change, and the homogeneity-of-slopes test stays the model-based F test. In anova_ancova() and in a Gaussian anova_glm(), comparisons that use robust standard errors keep the model’s residual degrees of freedom, and a note warns that with very small groups of unequal variance they can be anti-conservative; for a one-way design without covariates, anova_welch() is better calibrated.

Robust standard errors and weights

With frequency weights the sandwich is computed per observation, as it would be on the data expanded to one row per observation. sandwich::vcovHC() applied to the weighted rows directly would count each row as one unit with an inflated score, and overstate the standard errors:

table_hc3 <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                       success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3",
                       plots = FALSE)
appl_hc3 <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                      success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3",
                      plots = FALSE)
naive <- sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(from_table$model, type = "HC3")))[-1]
data.frame(comparison = table_hc3$effect_sizes$comparison,
           model_based = from_table$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_table = table_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_rows = appl_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_row_by_row = unname(naive))
#>       comparison model_based  hc3_table   hc3_rows hc3_row_by_row
#> 1 Female vs Male  0.08084646 0.08045399 0.08045399       1.497407
#> 2         B vs A  0.10983890 0.11002565 0.11002565       3.751704
#> 3         C vs A  0.10663289 0.10631318 0.10631318       2.786957
#> 4         D vs A  0.10582342 0.10528448 0.10528448       2.821575
#> 5         E vs A  0.12611350 0.12648471 0.12648471       2.911143
#> 6         F vs A  0.16998176 0.16944692 0.16944691       2.843432
grep("frequency weights represent", table_hc3$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "The robust covariance (HC3) treats each of the 4,526 observations the frequency weights represent as a unit, as it would on the data expanded to one row per observation; computed row by row it would count each row as one unit with an inflated score, and overstate the standard errors."

The HC3 standard errors from the table and from one row per applicant are the same. sandwich::vcovHC() on the table is wrong by a factor of 17 to 34.

With any other weights (sampling weights, precision weights, trials) the robust covariance treats each row as one independent unit, and $notes says so. If such weights in fact count identical observations, expand the data to one row per observation first.

When the model-based covariance is used instead

In some fits a sandwich covariance is wrong, and the function uses the model-based covariance instead, with a note saying why. That happens when:

  • the sandwich package is not installed;
  • some fitted values are on the boundary: a group with no events or all events in a binomial model, a group of all-zero counts, or a separated coefficient, where the sandwich collapses towards zero and gives spuriously small p-values;
  • a row has leverage 1, as a group or cell with a single observation does, so its residual is zero by construction and the sandwich would give a standard error of zero (HC0, HC1) or none at all (HC2 to HC4);
  • the robust covariance fails or has non-finite entries.

A site where nothing happened puts the fitted rate on the boundary:

incidents <- data.frame(
  site = rep(c("north", "south", "east"), each = 8),
  events = c(2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 3, 2, 4,
             6, 3, 5, 7, 4, 6, 5, 8,
             0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0))
grep("Robust", anova_count(incidents, "events", "site", vcov_type = "HC3",
                           plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Robust standard errors (HC3) were not used: some fitted values are on the boundary (a group with no events, or all events), where the sandwich covariance collapses towards zero and reports spuriously small p-values. Model-based standard errors were used instead."

A group with one observation has leverage 1:

small <- data.frame(g = c(rep("a", 6), rep("b", 6), "c"),
                    y = c(1:6, 3:8, 4))
grep("Robust", anova_glm(small, "y", "g", vcov_type = "HC3",
                         plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Robust standard errors (HC3) were not used: 1 row has leverage 1 (the model fits it exactly, as it does a group or cell with a single observation), so its residual is zero by construction and the sandwich would give the parameters it determines a standard error of zero (HC0, HC1) or none at all (HC2 to HC4). Model-based standard errors were used instead."

In anova_ancova(), car::Anova() refuses robust Wald tests for a model with aliased coefficients (an empty cell of the design, for example). $anova then keeps the model-based F tests, and $notes says so, while $emmeans and $posthoc still use the robust covariance.

See also

  • Binary outcomes: anova_bin(), Counts and rates: anova_count() and Any GLM family: anova_glm() for weights in each function, including precision weights on averages in a Gamma model.
  • ANCOVA: anova_ancova() for robust tests alongside the homogeneity-of-slopes test.
  • Diagnostics for the overdispersion, separation and sparse-data checks mentioned here.
  • Working with results for $notes, $data_used and $n_removed.
